title: Phoneme and allophone

sides.name: Phoneme
points: The smallest unit in a language that can convey a distinction in meaning.
Proved by a minimal pair, such as CAUGHT and COT for a speaker who keeps them apart.
Written in slashes, as in /p/.

sides.name: Allophone
points: One of the different phones that realize the same phoneme.
No minimal pair separates it from the other realizations, as with [stɑp̚] and [stɑpʰ].
Written in square brackets, as in [pʰ] or [p̚].

why: Two sounds can be clearly different to the ear and still be one phoneme. Only a change in meaning makes them separate phonemes.

title: Broad and narrow transcription

sides.name: Broad transcription
points: Uses slashes, as in /p/ and /b/.
Records the phonemes of an utterance.
Here voicing is a contrast that can be realized in several ways, such as aspiration or the timing in “writer” and “rider.”

sides.name: Narrow transcription
points: Uses square brackets, as in [pʰ] and [p].
Includes as much detail about the actual pronunciation as possible.
Here a phone is voiced only if the vocal folds vibrate during the whole sound.

why: The two notations answer different questions, so the word voicing means something different in each.

title: Derivational and inflectional morphology

sides.name: Derivational morphology
points: Creates new words, such as the verb knife from the noun or certification from certificate.
Productive only in limited ways, so friendhood is not a word.
Meaning is only partly predictable, as with neighborhood.
Never required by syntax.

sides.name: Inflectional morphology
points: Changes the form of the same word, such as knife and knives or knife and knifes.
Highly productive, but not always regular, as in mice and sang.
Meaning is predictable, such as plural or past tense.
Required by syntax, as when “two” forces a plural noun.

why: The difference explains why “needer” in a speech error is a derived noun while the -s in “learns” is an inflection the frame requires.

title: Syntactic roles and semantic roles

sides.name: Syntactic roles
points: Describe grammatical positions such as subject and object.
The subject is the noun phrase that controls the verb.
Change between “I have eaten the plums” and “The plums were eaten by me.”

sides.name: Semantic roles
points: Describe who did what to whom, such as Agent, Undergoer and Location.
The Agent is whoever performs the action.
Stay the same in both sentences, with me as Agent and the plums as Undergoer.

why: English usually puts the agent in the subject position, which is why “me” in a passive can wrongly feel like the subject.

title: Frequency effects and repetition priming

sides.name: Frequency effect
points: Comes from how often a word has been met over a lifetime.
Explained by experience tuning up activation dynamics, through a higher baseline, stronger connections or a changed threshold.
A lasting property of the word.

sides.name: Repetition priming
points: Comes from seeing the same word very recently.
Explained by leftover activation, because activation falls off more slowly than it rises.
A short-lived effect of the experimental environment.

why: Both make a word easier to activate, but one reflects accumulated learning and the other reflects activation that has not yet decayed.

title: Direct semantic priming and mediated priming

sides.name: Direct priming
points: Prime and target are directly associated, like lion and tiger.
Activation travels one step along a weighted connection.
Balota and Lorch found it in both lexical decision and pronunciation.

sides.name: Mediated priming
points: Prime and target are linked only through a third word, like lion and stripes through tiger.
Activation must travel two steps through the network.
Balota and Lorch found it in pronunciation but not in lexical decision.

why: Mediated priming is the stronger test of spreading activation, because no direct association can explain it.

title: Bottom-up and top-down processing

sides.name: Bottom-up
points: Activation flows from features to letters to words.
Driven by the input, so a clearer stimulus gives more activation.
Explains why LION is identified sooner as the noise mask fades.

sides.name: Top-down
points: Activation flows from words back down to letters.
Driven by stored knowledge, so an active word supports the letters that fit it.
Explains pattern completion of a partly hidden letter in WORK, and mishearings like malapropisms.

why: Recognition combines both directions, which is why expectations can fill in, or distort, what we perceive.

title: Tan and Wernicke’s patient

sides.name: Tan (Broca, 1861)
points: Speech was almost absent, with only one jargon syllable.
Seemed to understand what was said.
Lesion included the left inferior frontal gyrus, later found to reach deep into the insula.

sides.name: Wernicke’s patient
points: Speech was fluent.
The speech was meaningless gibberish.
Studied in the 1870s, when Wernicke and Lichtheim explained aphasias as disconnections between centers.

why: Together the cases suggested that producing speech and producing meaningful speech can break down separately.

title: Lesion studies and metabolic imaging

sides.name: Lesion studies
points: Show what behavior looks like after a region is damaged.
Now located with anatomical imaging instead of waiting for autopsy.
Tell us only indirectly what the intact region does.

sides.name: Metabolic imaging
points: Studies the brain in action with PET or fMRI.
Measures an index of oxygen consumption, slowly and at millimeter resolution.
Needs a control condition and subtraction logic, because the brain is always active.

why: Both methods depend on well-defined cognitive operations, and neither escapes Hughlings Jackson’s warning that locating damage is not locating function.

title: Behaviorism and the Cognitive Revolution

sides.name: Behaviorism (Skinner)
points: Language is verbal behavior learned by operant conditioning.
New responses come from stimulus generalization along concrete similarity.
Speech is explained by stimulus control from the environment.

sides.name: Cognitive Revolution (Chomsky)
points: Language is an internalized grammar of abstract rules.
New sentences are recognized because the grammar generates them, not because they resemble old ones.
The tractable question is the structure of what people say, studied through grammaticality judgments.

why: Chomsky’s critique made internal states legitimate again, because only a grammar could explain judgments about an infinite number of new sentences.

title: The GOFAI tradition and the emergentist tradition

sides.name: GOFAI, modular, Chomskyan
points: Linguistic knowledge is abstract and symbolic.
Language is treated as a Type I problem, so the implementational level can be set aside.
The job is to study how abstract knowledge interfaces with perception, memory and action.

sides.name: Emergentist, functionalist
points: Rule-like behavior emerges from statistical learning.
Implementation matters, with distributed representations and gradual learning.
The job is to study language use and relate it to general psychology.

why: The traditions disagree about where an explanation of language should start, with an abstract grammar or with the system that learns and uses it.

title: Anticipation, perseveration and metathesis

sides.name: Anticipation
points: A later sound comes in too early.
“Week long race” becomes “reek long race.”
Activation comes from what the speaker is about to say.

sides.name: Perseveration
points: An earlier sound repeats too late.
“John gave the boy” becomes “John gave the goy.”
Activation remains from what the speaker just said.

sides.name: Metathesis
points: Two sounds swap places.
“Keep a tape” becomes “teep a cape.”
Both sounds are active at once within the planned stretch of speech.

why: The direction of the slip reveals which source of activation won the competition.

title: Word exchanges and sound exchanges

sides.name: Lemma or word exchange
points: Whole lemmas swap slots while the frame stays the same.
“Where’d I bring it when I put it in” or “a language needer learns.”
Affixes and tense stay in their slots and attach to the new root.
Arises while the positional level is being filled.

sides.name: Sound exchange
points: Single phonemes swap within or across words.
“Vollowing fowel” for “following vowel.”
The words stay in place and only their sounds move.
Arises at phonological encoding, and the result is neat.

why: Because the two kinds of exchange preserve different things, they are evidence for separate levels of lemmas and phonemes.

title: Phonological encoding errors and speech gesture errors

sides.name: Phonological encoding error
points: The phonemes are put in the wrong order.
Neat, because the result follows English phonotactics and is clearly produced.
Examples are “Chomsky and Challe” and “with this wing I do red.”

sides.name: Speech gesture error
points: The motor system executes the planned phonemes imprecisely.
Not necessarily neat, so the speech comes out unclear.
“Odd hack” for “ad hoc” could be this kind or a metathesis.

why: Whether an error is neat or sloppy helps place it at the planning level or the movement level.

title: Word frequency and word length as causes of naming speed

sides.name: Frequency
points: How often a word is encountered.
Frequent names are named faster, in a log-linear relationship.
Still produced a robust effect when length was matched.

sides.name: Length
points: How long a word is.
Inversely related to frequency, so frequent words are short.
Was the confound that could have explained the original result.

why: Matching long high-frequency words with short low-frequency words separated the two, which is why frequency effects are not length effects in disguise.

title: Activation and selection

sides.name: Activation
points: Spreads from duck to related items like fish.
Helps recognition, so a related prime speeds identifying a word.
Produces identity priming, which speeds naming over cycles.

sides.name: Selection
points: Picks one lemma out of all the active ones.
In WEAVER++, depends on the target’s share of the total activation.
Produces semantic blocking, which slows naming in homogeneous sets.

why: The same spread of activation can speed recognition and slow production, because production must choose among competitors.

title: Gaze duration and eye-to-speech lag

sides.name: Gaze duration
points: How long the eyes stay on an object.
Tied to lemma selection.
Showed a blocking effect after the first cycle.

sides.name: Eye-to-speech lag
points: Time from the eyes leaving an object to its name starting.
Tied to phonological encoding and gesture planning, which continue without visual support.
Showed no significant blocking effect.

why: Because only gaze duration showed the cost, semantic blocking is placed at lemma selection.
